tip: The verb 'assistir' takes 'a' when it means to watch: 'assistiria ao filme', not 'assistiria o filme'.
'Pela qual' is 'por' plus 'a qual', literally "by which"; Portuguese says 'a razão pela qual' for "the reason why".
'Programa' is masculine even though it ends in '-a': 'o programa que assistimos'.
The preposition 'a' plus the article 'a' contracts to 'à' before a feminine noun: 'nós iríamos à praia'.
The verb 'pensar' takes 'em', not 'de', and 'em' plus 'o' becomes 'no': 'pensar no assunto' = think about the matter.
'Quem' can mean "whoever": 'quem não arrisca não petisca' is a set proverb, literally "whoever doesn't risk doesn't snack".
With 'nunca' before the verb, no second negative is needed: 'nunca esquecerei' = I will never forget.
'Fazer aniversário', literally "to make a birthday", is the set phrase for having one: 'vai fazer aniversário'.
Plain 'mudar' means to change; with the pronoun 'se', 'se mudar' means to move house: 'vão se mudar para Curitiba'.
'Tinha' plus a past participle marks an action done before another past moment: 'tinha cozinhado' = had cooked.
'Dar certo' is the fixed phrase for to work out or turn out fine: 'vai dar tudo certo' = it'll all work out.
'Haverá' is the formal "there will be"; everyday speech would say 'vai ter uma festa' instead.
'Ter que' plus an infinitive expresses obligation: 'vão ter que esperar' = you'll have to wait.
To name the color something is painted, use 'de' plus the color: 'pintado o quarto de branco' = painted the room white.
'Com' plus a noun often replaces an '-mente' adverb: 'com cuidado' = carefully, literally "with care".
'Ligar' meaning to phone someone takes 'para': 'tinha ligado para o médico' = had called the doctor.
'A gente' means we but takes a singular verb: 'a gente vai', never 'a gente vão'.
For a point in time, careful Portuguese uses 'em que', not bare 'que': 'o momento em que ele chegou' = the moment when he arrived.
The preposition 'a' plus 'o' contracts to 'ao': 'iremos ao evento' = we will go to the event.
In Brazilian Portuguese the pronoun normally goes before the infinitive: 'vou me inscrever', not 'vou inscrever-me'.
After 'até', Portuguese can use an infinitive that names its own subject: 'até ela chegar' = until she arrives.
After 'quando' about the future, the verb takes a special form: 'ser' becomes 'for', as in 'quando for necessário' = when it is necessary.
'Será que' opens a speculative question, like "I wonder if" or "do you think": 'será que ele vai aceitar o convite?'
In careful Portuguese, the 'de' of 'gostar de' moves in front of 'quem': 'a pessoa de quem eu gosto' = the person I like.
After a preposition you can use 'a qual' or 'o qual': 'por' plus 'a qual' becomes 'pela qual' = along which.
'Participar' takes 'de', and 'de' plus 'o' becomes 'do': 'participar do churrasco' = take part in the barbecue.
'Ir embora', not plain 'ir', is the set phrase for to leave: 'vão embora?' = are you leaving?
'Onde' means where and normally refers to places: 'o museu onde vimos' = the museum where we saw.
'Tenho' plus a participle isn't a one-time past; it means ongoing and repeated lately: 'tenho dormido mal' = I've been sleeping badly.
In 'se' (if) sentences about the unreal, '-ar' verbs take '-asse': 'falar' becomes 'falasse', as in 'se ela falasse' = if she spoke.
